title.en: Small-Business Website Checklist Before the Quote | Weissmann

metaDescription.en: Define audience, offer, legal pages, proof, tracking and ownership before any Swiss website quote. A fill-in brief you can hand to any agency or freelancer.

kicker.en: AI Marketing, SEO & GEO · Pre-Design Brief

h1.en: The Small-Business Website Checklist Swiss Agencies Rarely Show Before the Quote

answerFirst.en: Before requesting a website quote, a small Swiss business should define eight things itself: who the site is for, what it actually sells, the one action each page should drive, the legal pages Switzerland requires (an Impressum with identity and contact details, plus a privacy notice), what proof of trustworthiness already exists, who will own the analytics and tracking accounts, the local details a visitor needs (address, +41 number, opening hours, languages served), and who owns the photos, copy, domain and login credentials once the project ends. Agencies rarely ask for all of this upfront; deciding it yourself first turns a vague conversation into a comparable, checkable quote from any vendor.

heading.en: The Mockup Arrives Before the Decisions Do

paragraphs.en: Illustrative scenario: A physiotherapy practice in Winterthur asks an agency for a new website on a Monday. By Wednesday, a mockup arrives: clean typography, a calm colour palette, a photo of hands mid-treatment. The owner likes it immediately, the way you like a well-lit photograph of a menu. Then she reads it again, more slowly, and notices what is missing. Nobody asked which of her three treatment types actually fills her calendar. Nobody asked what should happen the moment someone lands on the homepage, or where her Impressum should live, or whose name the domain would be registered under. The site looks finished. The decisions behind it were never made.

This is not a story about a careless agency. It is the ordinary shape of most small-business website projects in Switzerland: a proposal arrives before a set of decisions does, because those decisions were always the client's job, not the designer's, and a written brief looks like homework until the day it is missing. What follows is that brief, in a form built to be filled in directly rather than read and admired: eight things worth deciding before a single quote is requested, whatever you eventually decide to build with — an agency, a freelancer, a website builder, or Weissmann's own Starter package.

heading.en: Why Agencies Skip These Questions, and What It Costs Later

paragraphs.en: A proposal that opens with “before I can price this, tell me who buys from you, what proof of trust you already have, and who will own your domain login” reads as friction to someone comparing three quotes on speed and turnaround. So most sales conversations default to questions that produce a number quickly — how many pages, which colours, what deadline — and design proceeds on whatever the client happens to volunteer, rather than on decisions the client was actually given room to make. None of this is dishonesty. It is what a sales process optimised for a fast, comparable quote looks like, and it quietly moves the real decisions into the middle of the project, exactly where changing an answer costs a revision round instead of five minutes of writing.

Weissmann's own website process states plainly that it starts with goal, audience and structure before a line of code is written — which is the right instinct, and exactly what this brief assumes ought to happen everywhere. But even a vendor that asks the right questions cannot answer them for you. Audience, offer and what counts as proof of trust are decisions only the business owner can make; the best a good process can do is ask early, instead of discovering the gap during a review call in week three.

heading.en: What Actually Goes Wrong When Nobody Wrote This Down

paragraphs.en: None of the following requires an incompetent vendor. It is simply what tends to happen when decisions get made implicitly, under deadline, by whoever happens to be in the room.

bullets.en: Wrong pages get built first: five general pages for a business whose actual sales come from one detailed service page and a booking form, discovered only after launch, when nobody converts and nobody can say why.

One page, three competing calls to action: a phone number, a contact form and a newsletter signup given equal visual weight, so a visitor takes the easiest option — leaving — instead of the one that would have generated an enquiry.

The legal notice becomes an afterthought: a placeholder line copied from a template, missing the correct legal form or a real contact address, discovered only when someone complains rather than when it was written.

Analytics gets created under the vendor's own account: years of visitor history leave with the agency the day the relationship ends, because nobody specified whose account it should have been from day one.

Proof of trust launches empty: reviews scattered across Google, an old Facebook page and a drawer of paper thank-you notes never make it onto the site, because nobody gathered them before the brief was due.
Ownership gets discovered, not agreed: photos and copy remain the vendor's property under a licence nobody read closely, found only when a second vendor is later asked to update the site.

heading.en: Eight Answers Only You Can Give

paragraphs.en: Fill in the eight sections below yourself, in a few sentences each, before you send a single enquiry. None of it requires design skill, technical knowledge or a finished brand — only decisions about your own business that nobody else is in a position to make for you.

heading.en: 1. Audience: The One Visitor This Site Has to Convince

paragraphs.en: A site trying to speak to everyone tends to convince no one quickly enough to matter, in a medium where most visitors decide whether to stay within seconds.

bullets.en: Describe your single most valuable visitor by situation, not demographic: “a facilities manager comparing three cleaning contractors on a Tuesday afternoon,” not “SMEs in the greater Zurich area.”

Note what that visitor already believes or doubts about a business like yours before they land on the page — are they price-shopping, worried about reliability, unsure whether you even serve their canton?
Note the device and moment they are most likely using: searching on a phone outside a competitor's premises, or reading calmly at a desk after a colleague's recommendation.

heading.en: 2. Offer: What You Sell, in the Words a Customer Uses

paragraphs.en: Many small-business sites describe capabilities in the language of the industry, not the problem a visitor is actually trying to solve when they search.

bullets.en: Write your single most bookable service or product in one plain sentence, the way a customer would search for it — not the way your industry describes it internally.
List two or three things people ask about that do not deserve their own page yet; grouping them saves you paying for five thin pages that split relevance instead of one strong one.
Note anything you deliberately do not offer, so the site does not invite the wrong enquiries — “no emergency callouts,” “no walk-ins without an appointment.”

heading.en: 3. Calls to Action: The One Thing Each Page Should Get Someone to Do

paragraphs.en: A page offering four actions at once — call, email, book, download a brochure — usually gets none of them, because equal emphasis reads as no emphasis at all.

bullets.en: Name the single primary action for your homepage, and be ready to say why it beats the others for your business specifically.
Decide honestly whether a phone call is your preferred first contact — common for Swiss trades and clinics — or a friction point you would rather route around with a form instead.
Decide what happens within one business day of that action being taken; a defined next step, not a vague promise, is what turns a form into something worth submitting.

heading.en: 4. Legal Pages: The Impressum Switzerland Actually Requires

paragraphs.en: Swiss law places a real, general obligation here. Under the Federal Act Against Unfair Competition, a business offering goods or services electronically must give clear and complete information about its identity and a contact address — commonly called an Impressum or legal notice — and wherever the site collects personal data, from a contact form to an analytics tool, a separate privacy notice is required under Swiss data protection law. This is a genuine requirement stated simply, not detailed legal advice on the exact wording your specific business needs; confirm the details with a Swiss lawyer or trust adviser, particularly if you operate as a registered company with more than one owner.

bullets.en: Confirm your exact legal name and legal form as registered, not a trading name, plus a real postal address and a working way to make contact.
Decide who is responsible for keeping the privacy notice current as tools change — a new analytics script, a new booking widget — because an unclear owner is the usual reason these notices go stale.
If you operate across languages or cantons, confirm the legal notice appears in every language version of the site, not only the main one.

heading.en: 5. Reviews and Proof: What Already Exists, Gathered in One Place

paragraphs.en: Most small businesses have more proof of trust than they realise; it rarely reaches a new site because nobody assembled it before the brief was written.

bullets.en: List every place a customer could currently leave, or already has left, a review — Google Business Profile, an industry directory, Facebook — and confirm who holds the login for each.

Gather two or three specific, honest outcomes you can describe without inventing a quote nobody actually gave: “reopened four business days after a burst pipe” persuades more than “excellent service.”
If you genuinely have no reviews yet, decide now how you will start asking for the first few once the new site is live, rather than leaving an empty “what clients say” section indefinitely.

heading.en: 6. Tracking and Analytics: Whose Account This Actually Is

paragraphs.en: The common mistake is not skipping analytics; it is letting a vendor create Google Analytics 4 and Search Console under their own account, so your visitor history leaves with them if the relationship ever ends.

bullets.en: Decide who creates the GA4 property and Search Console account before the project starts — it should be an account your business controls, with the vendor added as a user, never the reverse.
Name the one number you actually want to see monthly — enquiries submitted, calls started, bookings completed — so tracking measures an outcome, not just traffic.
Note any existing tracking, such as an old analytics account or a social pixel, that should carry over rather than be quietly abandoned when the new site launches.

heading.en: 7. Local Details: What a Visitor Needs to Find and Trust You

paragraphs.en: Small, easy to overlook, and disproportionately damaging when inconsistent.

bullets.en: Confirm the exact form of your phone number — a +41 landline, a mobile line answered by staff, a dedicated line for the website — and who genuinely answers it.

List your address exactly as it should appear everywhere it is used: Google Business Profile, the site footer, the legal notice. Inconsistent versions across these three quietly weaken local search visibility.
Note every language your actual customers use day to day, not only the official language of your canton, and decide which of them the site truly needs at launch versus later.

heading.en: 8. Content Ownership: Decide This Before You Ask for a Quote

paragraphs.en: The question worth settling before you approach anyone, not after a disagreement: if the relationship ended tomorrow, could you take your domain, your written content, your photos and your logins to a different vendor without a fight? State your expectation in the brief itself, so it is a starting condition of the quote rather than a clause you discover during contract review later.

bullets.en: State that the domain must be registered to your business, not the vendor's account, regardless of who pays the renewal invoice.
State whether you expect the written copy and photography to become your property on final payment, and get the answer in writing rather than implied by a friendly tone.
State that you expect real admin access to the CMS, hosting and analytics accounts at handover — not a promise to “reach out if anything comes up” later.

heading.en: Where You Can Safely Shorten This Brief

paragraphs.en: A sole trader building a single page through a simple builder, with no staff and no bookings, can reasonably spend ten minutes on this instead of an hour — there is no vendor relationship to unwind, so the ownership section shrinks to almost nothing. A business that already runs a documented brand guide and its own analytics governance has likely answered several of these sections in more depth than this brief asks for; use it to spot gaps rather than relitigate decisions already made properly. The one section worth completing regardless of how small the project is: legal pages. The Impressum obligation does not shrink with the size of the website.

heading.en: How a Finished Brief Turns Into an Actual Scope

paragraphs.en: A completed brief does more than make you an easier client; it makes a quote genuinely comparable. Weissmann's own process, for instance, starts with goal, audience and structure before any code is written — a finished brief is effectively that conversation, done in advance and in writing, which is why it tends to shorten the initial call rather than replace it. It also clarifies scope quickly: the current Starter Website package covers up to five core pages, one language and two defined rounds of revision, at a current promotional price of CHF 880 against a regular price of CHF 2,490 — a reasonable fit for a brief that lands on one visitor type, one core offer, one primary call to action and one language. A brief that reveals three customer segments, four services each needing its own detail page, or bilingual content from day one points toward a larger project instead, and it is better to know that before a quote arrives than after.

None of this requires working with Weissmann specifically. The same eight answers make any agency's, freelancer's or builder's proposal easier to judge, because you are comparing what each of them offers against decisions you already made — not against each other's sales pitch.

heading.en: Send the Brief Before You Send the First Email

paragraphs.en: A finished website is really the sum of eight smaller decisions a business owner has to make regardless of who ends up building it. Skipping them does not make them disappear; it just moves them inside the project, where every changed answer costs a revision round instead of five minutes of writing. Fill in the eight sections above — on paper, in a document, or in the interactive version built to accompany this article — before you send a single enquiry, and hand the finished brief to whichever vendor you end up asking for a quote, Weissmann included.

q.en: Does filling in this brief replace an initial conversation with an agency?

a.en: No — it is what makes that conversation useful instead of exploratory. A good discovery call still happens; it simply starts from your written answers instead of spending its time extracting them from you for the first time, which is where a surprising amount of a quote's turnaround time quietly goes.

q.en: I do not have any reviews yet. What do I put in that section?

a.en: Write down what you can honestly demonstrate instead — years in business, a specific outcome for a real client described without a fabricated quote, or a professional membership — and decide how you will start collecting reviews once the new site is live, so the section has a plan rather than staying empty indefinitely.

q.en: Do I need a lawyer to write my Impressum?

a.en: Not necessarily for a straightforward sole proprietorship, but the identity and contact details still need to be accurate and complete under Swiss unfair-competition law. If your structure is more complex — several owners, a regulated activity — a short check with a Swiss lawyer or trust adviser is worth the modest cost against getting it wrong.

q.en: What if some of my answers change after the site is built?

a.en: Some will, and that is normal — a brief fixes today's best answer, not a permanent one. The difference it makes is that changes after launch become deliberate updates you chose, rather than corrections to a guess nobody checked with you first.

q.en: Can I use this brief to compare quotes from more than one vendor?

a.en: Yes — that is one of its more useful side effects. Sending the same finished brief to two or three vendors lets you compare what each proposes against one fixed set of decisions, instead of comparing three quotes each built on a slightly different, half-formed conversation.

q.en: Does a simple five-page starter site need the same depth of answers as a larger project?

a.en: The questions stay the same; the answers get shorter. A five-page site still needs one audience, one clear offer, one primary call to action and a compliant legal notice — it just needs less detail in each than a twenty-page multilingual platform would.
